properties.title: Aquidneck Island gas outage from Algonquin pipeline pressure loss
properties.affected_jurisdiction: Newport and Middletown (Aquidneck Island), Rhode Island
properties.controlling_actor: Enbridge Inc. (Algonquin Gas Transmission) / National Grid
properties.trigger: On January 21, 2019 — one of the coldest days in a decade (2 deg F low) — high heating demand across the Algonquin pipeline system caused a low-pressure condition on the Aquidneck Island branch. A programming error in a valve at a meter station restricted flow, and a power failure at a local LNG backup facility removed the last safety net. Rhode Island DPUC called it a "perfect storm" but the root vulnerability was dependence on an interstate pipeline whose capacity allocation was not under local control.
properties.public_consequence: 7,455 gas customers lost heating service for up to 7 days in sub-freezing temperatures. Thousands displaced to hotels. Each customer required individual service restoration (relighting pilots). National Grid later paid a $2M class action settlement.
properties.one_line: Newport and Middletown lost heat for a week in freezing weather because their gas depends on a Canadian-owned interstate pipeline whose capacity allocation prioritized system-wide balance over a small island community.

sources.publisher: Rhode Island Division of Public Utilities and Carriers

properties.title: Colorado River post-2026 operating guidelines collapse leaves 40M people without agreed water rules
properties.affected_jurisdiction: Southern Nevada (Las Vegas); Central Arizona (Phoenix, Tucson); Southern California (MWD service area), Nevada / Arizona / California (most acutely)
properties.controlling_actor: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation / Upper Basin states (CO, WY, UT, NM)
properties.trigger: The 2007 Interim Guidelines governing Colorado River shortage-sharing expire end of 2026. Interior set a February 14, 2026 deadline for seven states to agree on successor rules. Upper Basin states refused to accept specific delivery cutbacks even during severe drought. The deadline was missed. Lower Basin proposed 27% cuts for AZ, 17% for NV, 10% for CA. No agreement reached. Tier 1 shortage in effect for 2026: Nevada gets 279,000 acre-feet (7% cut), Arizona loses 18%, California takes no cuts due to senior rights.
properties.public_consequence: 2.3 million people in Southern Nevada get 90% of water from the Colorado River. Arizona's 7.1 million residents face the largest proportional cuts. No agreed framework means the Interior Secretary may impose unilateral cuts. Municipal water providers cannot plan capital investments without knowing future allocations. 40 million people basin-wide affected.
properties.current_status: The seven basin states missed their deadline and the decision passed to the federal government. Reclamation published the Post-2026 Colorado River Reservoir Operations Final Environmental Impact Statement in the Federal Register on July 31, 2026, setting operations for Lake Powell and Lake Mead after the 2007 guidelines expire. For 2027-2028 it adopts the reductions the Lower Basin had proposed for itself; thereafter it revises guidelines at two-year intervals through 2036. It imposes no mandatory reductions on the Upper Basin. Each state was required to file a detailed conservation plan by August 2026.
properties.one_line: Forty million people across seven states depend on Colorado River water with rules expiring in 2026; Upper Basin refusal to accept cuts leaves Las Vegas and Phoenix exposed to allocation decisions made hundreds of miles away.

properties.title: Delmarva Peninsula customers hit with $183M capacity cost overcharge from flawed PJM auction parameter
properties.affected_jurisdiction: Delmarva Peninsula (statewide Delaware, Eastern Shore Maryland), Delaware / Maryland
properties.trigger: In the December 2022 capacity auction for 2024/2025, PJM's planning model predicted certain large plants and solar facilities would participate. When those suppliers declined, the inflated reliability requirement remained, producing anomalous results that drove up DPL South zone prices by ~$183M. PJM proposed a re-run; FERC approved a fix keeping higher prices. The D.C. Circuit Court vacated FERC's decision on January 13, 2026.
properties.public_consequence: DPL South zone customers faced $288.4M in capacity costs versus $110.7M under corrected parameters — a $178M overcharge driven by a modeling error at PJM. Delaware and Maryland regulators had no power to correct it and spent three years litigating through FERC and federal appeals court.
properties.one_line: A modeling error at PJM in Pennsylvania overcharged 515,000 Delmarva customers by $178M; state regulators had no power to fix it and litigated for three years.

properties.title: DOE Section 202(c) emergency orders socialize coal-retention costs across 11 MISO states
properties.affected_jurisdiction: 11 MISO states (cost-allocation footprint), MI, IN, IL, WI, MN, IA, MO, KY, AR, MS, LA
properties.trigger: DOE issued 43+ Section 202(c) emergency orders since May 2025 directing utilities to keep coal plants running past planned retirement against utility and state objection. Cumulative impact: ≥4.4 GW of coal capacity kept online as of April 2026. Notable: J.H. Campbell (Consumers Energy, MI; 1,560 MW; closure planned 15 years ahead of schedule), Centralia Unit 2 (WA; 730 MW; state SB 5769 mandated Dec 31 closure), R.M. Schahfer Units 17 & 18 (NIPSCO, IN; ~423 MW each; order extended through March 23, 2026).
properties.public_consequence: Compliance costs from a utility-by-utility order socialize across the regional RTO footprint. Consumers Energy reported $135M in Campbell compliance costs (end-May through Dec 2025) which it intends to recover from ratepayers across 11 MISO states — Michigan, Indiana, Illinois, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri, Kentucky, Arkansas, Mississippi, Louisiana — none of whom have any vote over the DOE order or the Michigan utility's retirement plan. The federal lever overrides state retirement timelines while pushing the bill outward through the RTO cost-allocation mechanism.
properties.current_status: Active litigation: Earthjustice challenge to Schahfer order; D.C. Circuit heard oral argument May 15, 2026 on Campbell-related challenge brought by states. Additional orders issued in PNW, Midwest, Mountain West (Dec 2025 batch ~2 GW). Pattern continues with no statutory limit on duration. By spring 2026 the same authority is also being deployed in PJM to direct backup generation at data centers and other large-load facilities during emergency conditions — a different operational pattern (dispatching at large loads, not blocking retirements) using the same statute. States and environmental groups argue DOE is using §202(c) to override normal RTO planning, resource-adequacy decisions, and cost-allocation rules without statutory limit.
properties.one_line: DOE keeps coal plants open against utility and state plans; the compliance bill gets allocated across 11 MISO states, including ones with no plant in their territory.

properties.title: New Orleans blackout exposes Entergy's multi-state transmission underinvestment under MISO governance
properties.affected_jurisdiction: Greater New Orleans (Orleans, Jefferson, St. Bernard, Plaquemines, St. Tammany parishes), Louisiana
properties.controlling_jurisdiction: New Orleans, LA (Entergy HQ) / Carmel, IN (MISO HQ), Louisiana / Indiana
properties.trigger: On May 25, 2025, MISO ordered Entergy to shed 498 MW of load across Greater New Orleans with only 30 minutes' warning after River Bend nuclear plant (1,035 MW) tripped and multiple gas plants were down. Entergy's four-state territory has blocked MISO long-range transmission planning — not one MISO LRTP line has been built in Entergy's territory, and MISO South planning won't begin until 2026 with earliest construction around 2036.
properties.public_consequence: 100,000+ customers lost power during Memorial Day weekend. The outage was not caused by extreme weather — it was a normal Sunday. The Amite South load pocket has had limited transmission import capability since at least 2006. New Orleans City Council regulates Entergy locally but has no authority over MISO's reliability decisions or Entergy's multi-state transmission investment priorities.
properties.one_line: 100,000 New Orleans customers lost power on an ordinary Sunday because Entergy has blocked MISO transmission planning across four states for a decade, leaving a known load pocket with insufficient import capacity.

properties.title: New England winter gas pipeline constraints causing electricity price spikes and reliability risk

properties.trigger: Gas pipelines into New England were sized for heating load alone. When natural gas generators (~50% of New England electricity) compete with heating customers for pipeline capacity on cold winter days, LDCs have contractual priority. In winter 2025-2026, DOE issued an emergency order (Jan 25 - Feb 14, 2026) allowing generators to exceed emissions limits to prevent blackouts. Natural gas prices on Jan 27, 2026 hit the highest level ever recorded in ISO-NE's pricing database (since 2003).
properties.public_consequence: Extreme wholesale electricity price spikes passed to ratepayers. Winter 2024/2025 wholesale energy market valued at $4 billion (up from $1.6B prior year). January 2026 wholesale power prices averaged $154.73/MWh real-time, with peaks reaching $441.80/MWh. Reliability risk during cold snaps requires emergency DOE orders, oil-fired backup, and reliance on globally-priced LNG.
properties.one_line: New England's gas pipelines were built for heating, not power generation; every cold winter, heating gets priority and 15 million electricity customers pay massive price spikes because no New England entity controls pipeline capacity decisions made by FERC-regulated interstate operators.

properties.title: Mississippi state government withheld federal relief funds, precipitating Jackson water system collapse
properties.trigger: In August 2022, Pearl River flooding overwhelmed the already-failing O.B. Curtis Water Treatment Plant. The deeper cause: Mississippi lawmakers withheld $1.8 billion in ARPA funds from Jackson despite urgent requests. Governor Reeves vetoed a bipartisan bill to help Jackson collect overdue water payments. The state health department failed to enforce Safe Drinking Water Act violations from 2015-2021, preventing federal intervention.
properties.public_consequence: 150,000-180,000 residents (84% minority, 25% below poverty line) lost safe drinking water for weeks. Boil-water advisories persisted for months. 55 pipe breaks per 100 miles annually (safe threshold: 15). ~50% of treated water lost to leaks or faulty meters. Total repair cost estimated at $2 billion. Federal disaster declaration issued.
properties.one_line: Jackson's 180,000 residents depend on a city water system whose survival requires state funding; Mississippi's government actively withheld federal relief dollars and vetoed revenue-recovery legislation.

properties.title: Potomac Interceptor sewer collapse releases 240M gallons of untreated sewage into Potomac River
properties.affected_jurisdiction: Loudoun County, Fairfax County, Town of Vienna, Town of Herndon, Montgomery County, Virginia / Maryland
properties.controlling_actor: DC Water (District of Columbia Water and Sewer Authority)
properties.trigger: A section of the 54-mile, 60-year-old, 72-inch Potomac Interceptor sewer line ruptured on January 19, 2026, along Clara Barton Parkway in Montgomery County, MD, near the C&O Canal National Historical Park. Virginia and Maryland suburbs send ~60 MGD of sewage through this DC Water-owned pipe they cannot maintain or inspect.
properties.public_consequence: ~240 million gallons of untreated wastewater released into the Potomac and its tributaries over 8 days — early estimates ranged as high as 300 million — one of the largest sewage spills in U.S. history. DC Water bypassed sewage through a dry stretch of the C&O Canal, itself polluting the national park. E. coli levels hundreds of times above EPA safety limits. Health advisories across DC, MD, and VA. Recreation shut down for months. Emergency bypass took five days; full flow not restored until March 14, 2026.
properties.current_status: April 20, 2026: DOJ (on behalf of EPA) and Maryland AG Anthony Brown + Maryland Department of the Environment filed parallel Clean Water Act complaints against DC Water in separate venues. Maryland seeks civil penalties up to $10,000/day per violation, cleanup costs, natural resource damages, and injunctive relief. May 20, 2026: DC Water disclosed that three additional segments of the 54-mile interceptor require urgent repair — the failure mode is not isolated to the original collapse location, and the maintenance backlog on the line that VA/MD suburbs depend on is broader than a single point of failure.
properties.one_line: Virginia and Maryland suburbs send sewage through a DC Water-owned pipe they cannot maintain; when it collapsed, 240 million gallons of untreated wastewater hit the Potomac over 8 days and triggered parallel federal and state lawsuits.

properties.title: Winter Storm Uri gas-electric interdependency collapse in Texas
properties.affected_jurisdiction: Statewide (Houston, DFW, San Antonio, Austin metros), Texas
properties.controlling_actor: ERCOT / Texas Railroad Commission / uncoordinated gas producers and pipeline operators
properties.trigger: February 2021 arctic blast caused cascading gas-electric interdependency failure. Permian Basin gas production dropped 85%. Gas compressors on interruptible electric contracts lost power during rolling blackouts, cutting gas supply to generators that needed gas to produce the electricity that powered the compressors. FERC/NERC found natural gas fuel supply issues accounted for 87% of all fuel-related generator outages.
properties.public_consequence: 4.5 million+ homes and businesses lost power, many for days (average 42 hours). Official death toll: 246; independent estimates: 426-978 excess deaths. 69% of Texans lost power; 49% lost water service. Economic losses estimated at $80-130 billion (Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas).
properties.one_line: Texas's unregulated gas producers had no obligation to winterize or coordinate with the electric grid; the freeze created a death spiral where electric outages killed gas compressors that killed gas supply that killed electric generators.
